Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Keep it ordinary: healthy isn’t happy all the time. If a student says they feel flat or low for weeks, follow up privately and connect them with a counselor.

Every student in the room

Families differ in how loud, close, private or family-first they are, and none of those is automatically healthier; some students also live with a diagnosis, and they can build real well-being too.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain that mental health and mental illness sit on two separate scales, name what healthy minds tend to do (bend, name feelings precisely, talk to themselves like a friend, repair), and turn one "stop doing that" goal into a trail they can steer toward. Healthy looks different across families, and the lesson says so.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minThree to stop, one to want more of: turn and talk, share out
  2. 7 minTwo scales, four boxes
  3. 5 minWhere should a mountain biker look?
  4. 6 minWhat healthy minds tend to do
  5. 6 minRock to trail
  6. 10 minFour situations: Lena, Nico, Chloe, you
  7. 6 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The stop-list turn and talk, the two scales, look where you want to go, rock to trail, two of the four situations, and the close.

Before you teach
Students with a diagnosis are in the room.

Say clearly that a student can have anxiety, depression or ADHD and still build real well-being. Treatment and a good life aren't either-or. The "coping and growing" quadrant is for them.

Don't make "healthy" a new standard to fail.

Healthy people feel the full range: sad, mad, worried. They come back to the window sooner. Keep the tone practical so nobody leaves feeling graded.

Languishing may land.

Some students will recognize "no diagnosis, but life feels hollow." That's useful. Offer one small step and a counselor for anyone who wants to talk it through.

If calm feels strange.

Students from loud or tense homes may find a calm relationship unfamiliar. Say it out loud: strange isn't the same as unsafe.

Know when it's heavier.

Hopelessness, feeling unsafe at home or with a friend or partner, or thoughts of not wanting to be here: walk the student to a counselor that day. 988 is there any time.

Let the bike analogy breathe.

If you ride, run or drive, tell your own version of looking at the rock and hitting it. Students remember the story better than the study.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Family styles differ.

Families differ in how much they share, how loud disagreements get, how much privacy is normal and how much family comes first. The test that works anywhere: can people disagree and stay connected?

Family-first is a gate, too.

Nico's card is there on purpose. Being home for dinner most nights can be a boundary a student chooses. Don't let the class call it unhealthy because it's different from their own family.

Diagnosis and disability.

Neurodivergent students and students with mental health diagnoses should see themselves in "coping and growing." Avoid any picture of healthy that means "no condition."

Borrowed pictures.

"Think of someone who handles hard moments well" might be a grandparent, coach, faith leader, older sibling or friend. Let students pick from their own world.

Language for feelings.

Some students have rich feeling words in a home language that English lacks. Invite them to use those; precise is what matters.

Money and stress.

Students carrying real pressures, like money at home or caring for family, can still flourish, and their stress isn't a personal failing. Keep "small turns" realistic for them.

What the research says

Mental illness and mental health are measured on two separate scales. Adults who were languishing were nearly six times as likely as flourishing adults to have a major depressive episode.

Keyes, Journal of Health and Social Behavior, 2002

In a national sample of 1,234 youth, flourishing was the most common category for ages 12 to 14; by 15 to 18, "moderately healthy" had overtaken it.

Keyes, American Journal of Orthopsychiatry, 2006

Drivers looked at a point on the inside of each curve one to two seconds before turning into it. Where they looked came first; steering followed.

Land and Lee, Nature, 1994

Psychological flexibility, shifting strategies when one stops working and acting on values when it's uncomfortable, is central to health.

Kashdan and Rottenberg, Clinical Psychology Review, 2010

People who can tell distinct negative feelings apart are less likely to turn to binge drinking, aggression or self-harm when upset.

Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight, Current Directions in Psychological Science, 2015

Across 19 studies of 7,049 people ages 10 to 19, self-compassion was strongly linked with lower anxiety, depression and stress.

Marsh, Chan and MacBeth, Mindfulness, 2018

The window of tolerance: the zone where you can feel something strongly and still think.

Siegel, The Developing Mind, 1999
